classification.difficultyReason: Read an edge weight and add the relevant weights in two practical networks.

content.prompt: The graphs below show details about air travel between Australian cities.

spec.description: Four-city undirected network. Ordinary source blue edges and red vertex markers are rendered black under house style. The Perth–Melbourne and Sydney–Adelaide edges cross without a vertex.
spec.mathematics: Perth–Sydney 5; Perth–Melbourne 5; Perth–Adelaide 3; Sydney–Adelaide 9; Sydney–Melbourne 27; Adelaide–Melbourne 9. Weights are flights per day.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertices, city names and weights are permanent student-visible givens.

spec.description: Same city positions and connectivity as the flights network, preserving the paired comparison. Ordinary source blue edges and red markers are rendered black. Crossing edges have no vertex.
spec.mathematics: Perth–Sydney 640; Perth–Melbourne 720; Perth–Adelaide 320; Sydney–Adelaide 950; Sydney–Melbourne 5040; Adelaide–Melbourne 950. Weights are maximum passengers per day.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertices, city names and weights are permanent student-visible givens.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many flights are available per day between Sydney and Adelaide?

answer.worked: The Sydney–Adelaide edge in the flights network has weight 9, so there are 9 flights per day.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many total flights are available between all these cities?

answer.worked:
Add each edge weight in the flights network once.

$$5+5+3+9+27+9=58$$

There are 58 flights per day in total.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is the maximum number of passengers per day that can fly out of Sydney?

answer.worked:
Add the capacities of the three edges connected to Sydney.

$$640+950+5040=6630$$

The maximum is 6630 passengers per day.
